newsitem.title: UK: Disney lights up Pocahontas resting place.
newsitem.headline: Disney lights up Pocahontas resting place.

text.p: The final resting place of Pocahontas, the American Indian princess who married an English settler, will be illuminated for the first time on Saturday thanks to a gift from the Disney film studio.

The white tower of St George's Church in Gravesend, near the mouth of the Thames estuary east of London, will be visible for miles when new floodlights are turned on this Saturday, named Pocahontas Heritage Day by the local council.

The floodlighting scheme was largely financed by a 9,000 pound ($14,090) donation from Buena Vista International, part of the Disney organisation that released a highly successful animated version of the Pocahontas story last year.
The daughter of an Indian chief who ruled over 40 tribes, Pocahontas won her place in American history by protecting the first English colonists from local tribes in the 17th century.
According to accounts by John Smith, leader of Jamestown, the first permanent British settlement in North America, Pocahontas saved his life after her tribe captured him.

Pocahontas was later kidnapped by the settlers and used as a bargaining chip for permanent peace. During her captivity she became the first native American to learn English, convert to Christianity and marry an Englishman, John Rolfe.
Known as Rebecca Rolfe, and mother of a baby son, Pocahontas was taken ill on board ship returning to America in 1617. She was landed at Gravesend and died there.
The present church dates from 1727 and the exact burial place of the princess is not known. St George's church has received a steady stream of visitors since the film was released. ($1=.6385 Pound)
